name: Tambora
confidence_why: Tambora is known only from the roughly 48-word list in Raffles 1817, and Donohue 2007, the sole analysis of it, states that suprasegmental features cannot be inferred while noting that the acute accents, which Raffles's own orthography key says mark emphatic syllables, would point to penultimate stress if they mark stress at all.
catalog_citation: Donohue, Mark. 2007. The Papuan Language of Tambora. Oceanic Linguistics 46(2): 520-537. doi:10.1353/ol.2008.0014 (UH Press typeset PDF, author's ANU page via an archived copy (Internet Archive, 2014-02-05); saved). Primary data: Raffles, Thomas Stamford. 1817. The History of Java, vol. II, Appendix F, comparative vocabulary, pp. cxcviii-cxcix (Wellcome scan, pp. 576-577; saved as and 220-dpi crops). Accent convention: Raffles 1817, vol. I, front matter 'Orthography', p. xiii (Wellcome scan, archive.org scan. grade open-text).
catalog_locator: Donohue 2007 p. 523: sec. 2, paragraph immediately preceding Table 1 (first sentence), and sec. 3 'Phonology', first two sentences; domain sentence p. 522, sec. 2, second paragraph. Raffles 1817 vol. I, 'Orthography', p. xiii (roman page number partly garbled in the scan as '(xi‘i)'): 'To avoid confusion, the emphatic syllables are alone accented, and the inherent Vowel a has invariably been adopted.'
catalog_quote: The function of the acute accent is not explained, but quite possibly represents erratic stress marking. [...] 3. PHONOLOGY. The phonology that we can infer is shown in table 2, consisting of 15 consonants and five vowels; suprasegmental features cannot be inferred, though if the frequent acute accents in Raffles's list indicate stress, it appears to be penultimate. Depending on the interpretation of the hyphen there might be a glottal stop as well. || Raffles 1817 vol. I, 'Orthography', p. xiii: The principles of Orthography, recommended by Sir William Jones, and adopted by the Asiatic Society at Calcutta, have been adopted in this work, with some slight modifications. The consonants preserve the same sounds generally as the same letters in the English alphabet: the vowels are used as in Italian. To avoid confusion, the emphatic syllables are alone accented, and the inherent Vowel a has invariably been adopted.

new_statements.citation: Donohue, Mark. 2007. The Papuan Language of Tambora. Oceanic Linguistics 46(2): 520-537. doi:10.1353/ol.2008.0014
new_statements.locator: p. 523 (sec. 2, paragraph preceding Table 1; and sec. 3 'Phonology', first sentence)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (19 pp., UH Press FrameMaker typeset, Internet Archive copy of the author's ANU page) and its. Both quoted sentences are present verbatim on p.523: the text 'The function of the acute accent is not explained, but quite possibly represents erratic stress marking.' (sec. 2, paragraph immediately before Table 1, after the p.523 running head) and the text '3. PHONOLOGY. The phonology that we can infer is shown in table 2, consisting of 15 consonants and five vowels; suprasegmental features cannot be inferred, though if the frequent acute accents in Raffles's list indicate stress, it appears to be penultimate. Depending on the interpretation of the hyphen there might be a glottal stop as…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only evidence is the acute accents Raffles (1817) printed on his ~48-word Tembora list, which Raffles never explains; Donohue reads them as (erratic) stress marks and observes that, if so, stress falls predominantly on the penultimate syllable (e.g. kutélin, koného, saróne, homóri, kokóre, simári, karáyi, moríhoh). He explicitly says suprasegmentals cannot be securely inferred from the corpus.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said (corpus is isolated words only).
new_statements.exceptions: None discussed by Donohue; the accent marking is called 'erratic' (some polysyllables unaccented, e.g. seena, yelai, maimpo, naido). A few accented forms in Raffles' list are not obviously penultimate depending on syllabification of vowel sequences/hyphens (kálae, báta-in, óna-yit, gónong vs gonóre), which Donohue does not comment on.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms only: single words elicited in 1810s and printed in a comparative vocabulary; no phrases or clauses exist for the language. Statement is an inference from a philological source, hedged as conditional.
new_statements.identity_note: Single variety; Raffles spells it 'Tembóra', Zollinger 'Tambora/Tembora'. Language extinct since the 1815 eruption; entire corpus is Raffles' 1817 ~48-word list (Appendix F, vol. II), so Donohue 2007 is and will remain the only linguistic analysis. Glottocode tamb1257, ISO xxt.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Donohue 2007 statement ('if the frequent acute accents in Raffles's list indicate stress, it appears to be penultimate'); it is the primary source Donohue inferred from. Refines it by supplying Raffles' explicit key that the accents mark emphatic syllables (vol. I 'Orthography'), the full accented list from the 1830 edition (identical forms to the 1817 edition already held by the project), and the two non-penultimate forms (báta-in, óna-yit). The catalog record for Tambora (world-r2-2026-09-17) has an empty rule; this supports filling it with 'penultimate (inferred from Raffles' accent marks)'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No prose on Tambora stress anywhere in vol. II; the evidence is the acute accents in the 48-item Tembora wordlist, which Raffles' own orthography note (vol. I) defines as marking 'the emphatic syllables'. Of the 28 accented forms, 26 carry the accent on the penultimate syllable (kutélin, kúmba, koného, saróne, sisaróne, simári, homóri, kokóre, sóntong, sumóre, kóngkong, tádung, gonóre, kilaíngkong, karáyi, moríhoh, mákan..). Read as emphatic = stressed, word stress is penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said; no form carries two accents (saing kóme and saing'óre are accented on the second element only).
new_statements.exceptions: báta-in and óna-yit carry the accent on the first of three syllables (penult of the base before -in in báta-; kude-in and sia-in with the same -in are unaccented). 20 of 48 forms carry no accent at all, including all monosyllables (nih, doh, ilah) and disyllables such as seena, kiro, naido, gonong, andik, ingkong, kingkong, hok-hok, so the marking is incomplete rather than systematic.
new_statements.identity_note: Raffles' 'Tembora' is the language of the Tambora kingdom on the northern peninsula of Sumbawa, recorded before the 1815 eruption; it is the sole primary record and the same list Crawfurd 1852 and Donohue 2007 analyse. Crawfurd's 'Tambora' and Raffles' 'Tembora' are the same list (Crawfurd says his numerals are 'taken from the Appendix to Sir Stamford Raffles' History of Java').
